full_query: A 55-year-old man presents to urgent care for weakness and weight loss. For the past several months, he has felt progressively weaker and has lost 25 pounds with intermittent abdominal pain. The patient has not seen a physician in 30 years and recalls being current on most of his vaccinations. A few years ago, he went to the emergency department due to abdominal pain and was found to have increased liver enzymes due to excessive alcohol use and incidental gallstones. The patient has a 50 pack-year smoking history. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 161/108 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam reveals an emaciated man. The patient has a negative Murphy sign and his abdomen is non-tender. Cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? (A) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (B) CT scan of the chest (C) HIDA scan (D) Right upper quadrant ultrasound (E) Smoking cessation advice and primary care follow up

(A) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis: This option is appropriate for evaluating the abdominal pain, assessing for potential malignancies such as hepatocellular carcinoma, pancreatic cancer, or other intra-abdominal pathology, given the patient's significant weight loss and alcohol history
(B) CT scan of the chest: Given the patient's significant smoking history, a CT scan of the chest could be indicated to rule out lung cancer
However, the primary symptoms (abdominal pain and weight loss) suggest an abdominal pathology first
(C) HIDA scan: Primarily used for diagnosing acute cholecystitis or other gallbladder function issues
Given the absence of acute gallbladder symptoms (negative Murphy sign, non-tender abdomen), this is less appropriate
(D) Right upper quadrant ultrasound: Useful for evaluating gallstones and liver pathology, but less comprehensive than a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
(E) Smoking cessation advice and primary care follow up: Important, but not the most critical immediate step given the concerning symptoms that require more urgent diagnostic evaluation
